group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 58-year-old man who lives alone in a two-bedroom condominium and still clocks forty hours a week as a city-bus mechanic arrived by private car to the emergency department shortly after noon, reporting four days of progressively heavier cough that turned rust-colored overnight, intermittent rigors, and a stabbing discomfort along the right costal margin whenever he tried to inhale fully; he deliberately skipped his morning lisinopril, furosemide, and sevelamer as well as his usual pre-shift coffee in order, in his words, “to let the numbers speak for themselves.” He denies pre-hospital acetaminophen, ibuprofen, inhalers, supplemental oxygen, or any intravenous fluids. His medical record lists a five-year history of ischemic cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction last measured at 30 %, along with stage-3 chronic kidney disease attributed to long-standing hypertension; outpatient serum creatinine has hovered in the upper 1.9 to low-2 mg/dL range for the past year without dialysis discussions. He has never been hospitalized for stroke, transient neurologic attacks, or hepatobiliary disorders, and he continues to maintain his own household chores without home-health assistance. Tobacco exposure totals twenty pack-years, but he quit eight years ago; alcohol is limited to a single can of beer on Saturday evenings, and he denies illicit drug use. Vaccination registry confirms both pneumococcal formulations and this season’s influenza shot. On arrival he sat bolt upright on the stretcher, conversing in complete sentences, correctly stating the date, location, and the outcome of the morning sports broadcast. Skin was warm, lightly diaphoretic, and capillary refill was brisk; no peripheral cyanosis or clubbing was noted. Untreated triage vital signs on ambient air at this sea-level facility were: oral temperature 38.3 °C, regular radial pulse 74 beats per minute confirmed on three-lead telemetry, automated right-arm blood pressure 129/76 mm Hg corroborated manually, respirations 25 breaths per minute with mild intercostal recruitment, and fingertip pulse oximetry oscillating between 90 % and 91 %. Jugular venous contour rose to the level of the clavicle but not above while seated at 45°, and there was trace pitting edema at both ankles consistent with baseline. Cardiac auscultation revealed a crisp S1 and S2 with a soft third sound already documented previously and no new murmurs. Pulmonary examination demonstrated absent breath sounds with stony dull percussion over the lower third of the right posterior hemithorax, bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles just superior to that zone, and resonant left-sided fields without wheeze. Abdomen was soft, mildly protuberant, nontender, and without organomegaly. A brief neurologic screen showed equal, reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, 5/5 strength throughout, and steady finger-to-nose testing. A capillary glucometer performed before vascular access measured 117 mg/dL. Peripheral venous samples and a right radial arterial puncture were obtained within ten minutes of bay entry, before any flushes larger than 3 mL of heparinized saline, antimicrobials, bronchodilators, diuretics, or crystalloid. Basic metabolic panel returned sodium 136 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, chloride 102 mEq/L, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 37 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, the azotemia aligning with his outpatient trend. Complete blood count revealed leukocytes 14.2 × 10⁹/L with 87 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 38 %, hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, and platelets 232 × 10⁹/L. Arterial blood gas on room air demonstrated pH 7.37, PaCO₂ 34 mm Hg, PaO₂ 77 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, depicting mild hypoxemia without significant acid–base disturbance. Serum lactate measured 1.8 mmol/L, and high-sensitivity troponin remained below assay threshold. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained fifteen minutes after arrival—before any therapy—showed dense consolidation in the right middle and lower lobes with air bronchograms accompanied by a concave fluid layer that obliterated the right costophrenic angle, findings consistent with a moderate reactive collection; cardiac silhouette matched prior imaging, and mediastinal contours were stable. Twelve-lead electrocardiography revealed sinus rhythm at 75 bpm with Q waves in the inferior leads unchanged from previous studies and no acute ST-segment shifts. Two peripheral sets of blood cultures, an induced sputum specimen, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila, and a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched to the laboratory before any antimicrobial or supportive medication was ordered. Up to the moment this narrative is entered, the patient has received no intravenous fluids, no vasoactive agents, no antipyretics, and no supplemental oxygen beyond the 21 % inspired fraction in the room, ensuring that every physiologic observation, laboratory value, and imaging finding above represents his untreated state at presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points using untreated admission findings.
1. Demographics: A man receives his age in points: 58. He lives independently, so the nursing-home adjustment is 0.
2. Comorbidities: Heart failure from ischemic cardiomyopathy adds 10; chronic kidney disease adds 10. No malignancy, liver disease, or cerebrovascular disease is reported (0 each).
3. Examination: He is oriented, RR 25 is below 30/min, systolic BP 129 is at least 90 mm Hg, temperature 38.3°C is neither <35 nor ≥40°C, and pulse 74 is below 125/min (0 each).
4. Laboratory findings: BUN 37 meets the ≥30 mg/dL threshold (+20), even though the azotemia is chronic. Arterial pH 7.37 is not <7.35, sodium 136 is not <130 mEq/L, glucose 117 is not ≥250 mg/dL, and hematocrit 38% is not <30% (0 each). Room-air PaO₂ 77 is not <60 mm Hg and saturation is not <90% (0).
5. Imaging: Right pleural effusion adds 10.
Total = 58 + 10 + 10 + 20 + 10 = 108 (PSI class IV).
Final answer: 108
